A 73-year-old previously healthy female (BMI 25.8), with a self-reported lower abdominal hernia for more than three years, presented with a one-day history of lower abdominal pain and vomiting. Physical examination revealed a firm, tender, irreducible bulge measuring approximately 10 × 5 cm in the right groin, located 3 cm above the pubic region and inferior to the inguinal ligament. The overlying skin appeared tense but without necrosis or ulceration (Figures 1A-1B). Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis, with a markedly elevated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR 10.7). Although C-reactive protein (CRP) was very low (<0.06 mg/dL) at presentation, early normal or low CRP does not exclude strangulation (Table 1). CT demonstrated a small bowel loop herniating through the right femoral canal, with a mesenteric whirl sign, consistent with an incarcerated femoral hernia and raising concern for strangulation (Figures 2A-2C). The interval from emergency department arrival to incision was approximately eight hours.

A 73-year-old previously healthy female (BMI 25.8), with a self-reported lower abdominal hernia for more than three years, presented with a one-day history of lower abdominal pain and vomiting. Physical examination revealed a firm, tender, irreducible bulge measuring approximately 10 × 5 cm in the right groin, located 3 cm above the pubic region and inferior to the inguinal ligament. The overlying skin appeared tense but without necrosis or ulceration (Figures 1A-1B). Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis, with a markedly elevated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR 10.7). Although C-reactive protein (CRP) was very low (<0.06 mg/dL) at presentation, early normal or low CRP does not exclude strangulation (Table 1). CT demonstrated a small bowel loop herniating through the right femoral canal, with a mesenteric whirl sign, consistent with an incarcerated femoral hernia and raising concern for strangulation (Figures 2A-2C). The interval from emergency department arrival to incision was approximately eight hours.

On admission, the patient received IV crystalloid resuscitation, multimodal analgesia, and antiemetics, and correction of electrolyte imbalance. Single-agent broad-spectrum prophylaxis was administered, together with mechanical venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Informed consent included the possibility of conversion to open surgery and temporary stoma formation.

Diagnostic laparoscopy revealed a segment of ileum incarcerated at the femoral canal. The loop was reduced and appeared dusky, with a 0.5 cm perforation, necessitating resection of approximately 5 cm of bowel located 50 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve. Mesenteric torsion was identified and corrected. Bowel continuity was restored extracorporeally through a 3-cm periumbilical mini-laparotomy, after which definitive hernia repair was performed via a TAPP approach using a macroporous polypropylene mesh (Optilene) (Figures 3A-3B). The patient’s postoperative recovery was uneventful, with oral intake resumed by day 4 and discharge on day 11.

summary.text: A previously healthy 73-year-old woman with BMI 25.8 and a self-reported lower abdominal hernia over three years presented with one day of lower abdominal pain/vomiting and a tender irreducible right groin mass ~10×5 cm, without skin necrosis/ulceration. Labs showed leukocytosis, neutrophil predominance, relative lymphopenia/NLR 10.7 and low CRP, with author-described preserved renal function and normal CPK. CT showed a small-bowel loop herniating through the right femoral canal with a mesenteric whirl sign, consistent with incarcerated femoral hernia and raising concern for strangulation; arrival-to-incision was ~eight hours. Authors state elevated NLR with obstructive features favored prompt surgical exploration over attempted manual reduction.

Admission fluids, analgesia, antiemetics, electrolyte correction and prophylaxis preceded laparoscopy. Dusky incarcerated ileum with body-reported 0.5 cm perforation (discussion says small perforation; Figure 3 caption instead says possible impending serosal defect; interpretation unresolved) required ~5 cm resection 50 cm proximal to ileocecal valve, torsion correction and stapled side-to-side extracorporeal anastomosis through a 3 cm mini-laparotomy. Contamination control preceded preperitoneal TAPP Optilene polypropylene mesh fixation and secure peritoneal closure in a stable/no-gross-spillage context. Optional ICG capability does not establish actual use.

ERAS and wound review were performed; oral intake resumed by day four and uneventful recovery led to day-eleven discharge. Follow-up was arranged at 30–90 days with contingent recurrence imaging. Authors mention limited follow-up but supply no specific recurrence or wound outcome.

evidence.quote: To provide further perspective, a contemporaneous case involving an incarcerated inguinoscrotal hernia was managed by conventional open exploration. The hernia sac contained a segment of ischemic transverse colon, and, due to the concern for contamination and uncertain bowel viability, a non-mesh Bassini repair with diverting loop colostomy was performed. This case illustrates the rationale for avoiding prosthetic material in clearly contaminated fields and highlights the traditional open approach as a still-relevant strategy. It also provides a useful contrast to the laparoscopic management strategy employed in our patient.

article_limitations: Caption claims and pixel observations are kept separate; the four actual JPEGs (750-px wide) were inspected by the Claude Sonnet 5.5 annotator audit and described in the visual submission; caption-only fields remain labelled as caption.
Contemporaneous inguinoscrotal comparison case treated as a separate original patient because it is explicitly narrated without a literature citation; sparse identity/outcome details remain unstated.
No explicit same-patient prior-report linkage identified. Literature series and proposed algorithm do not enlarge patient actions.

ICG fluorescence is optional/when available, not confirmed as performed. The consent possibility of open conversion or temporary stoma (b00021) is a contingency for the index patient; no conversion or stoma occurred in the index patient, while an actual diverting loop colostomy belongs only to the comparison patient p2.

Perforation wording differs across layers: operative "0.5 cm perforation", discussion "small perforation", Figure 3 caption "focal serosal defect with possible impending perforation", Figure 3A pixel label "Perforation or Serosal injury". Kept review-only and unreconciled; no invented time/stage/evolution.
Generic 3–5 cm mini-laparotomy range is superseded by actual reported 3 cm incision, without inventing another procedure.
30–90-day follow-up is mentioned but individual recurrence/wound findings are not supplied.
BMI unit unstated. Creatinine numeric flag unknown: preserved renal function is author interpretation, not range-derived normal assertion.

Optional ICG unconfirmed and conditional recurrence imaging separated from performed care. Booking 30–90 day followup is not inferred to occur after discharge; oral intake byday 4 is an upper-bound milestone.

Figure 4 is a background/proposed algorithm: printed thresholds "NLR >~6.5, D-dimer >300, CPK >140" have no printed units, and D-dimer, lactate and LDH are not reported for the index patient (no negative inferred); comparing index NLR 10.7 or CPK 106 to those thresholds is not an author statement here.

The second case (p2) is a one-paragraph contemporaneous inguinoscrotal hernia vignette (b00033) with no age, sex, dates, outcome, figure or citation; whether it is the authors' own patient is implied by "contemporaneous" and "our patient" contrast but not stated.
Follow-up at 30-90 days was arranged and recurrence imaging only planned; the conclusion's "follow-up ... is limited" supplies no completed visit or result.
